metaDescription: Six XLR streaming mixers compared on preamp gain, dual XLR inputs, faders, routing and DSP, so a real microphone sounds right on a live stream.
expertTake: The Elgato Wave XLR Pro is the best XLR streaming mixer here because two XLR inputs with 80 dB of gain each, onboard DSP and five hardware mixes handle a host and a guest. The FIFINE Ampligame SC3 is the value pick for one dynamic microphone. A streamer who is happy with a USB microphone does not need XLR at all.
introParagraphs: Moving a stream to XLR is the single biggest step up in voice quality available to a streamer. A real broadcast microphone rejects room noise better than a USB model, and it can be replaced or upgraded without touching the rest of the chain.

That step needs a mixer or interface that supplies clean gain and, for condensers, phantom power. The best streaming versions also add routing for game and chat audio, onboard processing and a way to control levels without opening a software window.

products.name: Elgato Wave XLR Pro dual XLR interface and mixer
products.description:
The Wave XLR Pro is built for two voices and a busy desk. Each of its two XLR inputs offers 80 dB of gain, enough for demanding dynamic microphones, and an onboard Wave FX processor runs DSP effects and VST plugins in one signal chain. Clipguard 2.0 is designed to catch peaks before they distort.

Its dual USB-C connections let a second computer, a console or a phone join the desk, and any input can be patched to any output through flexible routing and five hardware mixes. The tradeoff is that the mixing happens in software and on a small surface, so it lacks the row of faders that the MAONO G3 provides. It also sits at the premium end of the price range.

For a host and a guest, the practical setup is one microphone per input, a recording mix for the computer and a separate monitor mix for headphones. Save a profile per scene, keep the firmware current and listen to a test recording through speakers to confirm that the blend matches what the audience will hear.
products.bestFor: Two person streams and podcasts that want high gain, DSP and flexible routing.
pros: Two XLR inputs with 80 dB gain each
Onboard DSP and VST plugin support
Dual USB-C for a second PC or console
Five hardware mixes for flexible routing

products.name: RØDECaster Duo compact audio production studio
products.description:
The RØDECaster Duo puts a broadcast desk in a compact body: two Neutrik combo jacks with low noise, high gain preamps, four faders, a haptic touchscreen and six SMART pads with bank switching. It handles microphones and instruments and doubles as a USB interface for streaming.

Its strength is the hardware surface. Four faders under the hand beat any software mixer when a stream gets busy, and the pads trigger effects without a keyboard. The limit is the pair of inputs, so a third microphone needs another device, and the premium build puts it above most USB boxes in price. Against the Wave XLR Pro it offers faders and pads where Elgato offers more routing and a second USB-C link.

It rewards a little setup time. Map the pads to the sounds you actually use, save the routing for each show format and keep the firmware current through the unit's own menu. A short USB cable and balanced XLR leads keep the desk tidy.
products.bestFor: Two host streams that want faders, pads and a touchscreen in one box.
pros: Four faders on a compact body
Pads with bank switching expand effects
cons: Costs well above entry level boxes

products.name: MAONO G3 gaming mixer with 4 faders and 3 submixes
products.description:
The G3 is a desktop mixer and XLR interface that maps any audio source to one of four faders, so a streamer controls game, chat, music and microphone by hand. Three submixes let the stream, the headphones and a recording each carry a different blend.

The cost is configuration time and a Windows centric workflow. A streamer who needs only a microphone path will find the G3 overbuilt. Next to the Wave XLR Pro it provides more hands on control and one XLR input rather than two, so it suits a solo streamer with many sources rather than a duo.

Save routing profiles for each game, label the faders and check the stream mix with a short recording. Keep the unit on a direct USB port and back up the profile after changes.
products.bestFor: Solo streamers who balance several sources with one XLR microphone.
pros: Four faders map to any source
Three submixes for stream and headphones
XLR interface for a real microphone

products.name: MAONO G1 Neo gaming mixer with XLR, 48V and sound pads

specList.label: Bundle
specList.value: Also sold with a PD200XS dynamic mic

products.description:
The G1 Neo pairs a built in preamp and 48V phantom power with four custom sound pads, Bluetooth and a voice change feature. It is sold alone and in a bundle with a PD200XS XLR dynamic microphone, which makes it an easy first step into XLR.

The phantom supply means it can drive a condenser microphone, which many entry boxes do not list. The extras suit an entertainment stream more than a quiet talk show, and the box has a single microphone input. It sits between the SC3 and the G3 in control depth.

Load the pad clips once, keep them short and set their level below your voice. If you buy the bundle, the dynamic microphone is a sensible match for a noisy room.
products.bestFor: Streamers who want phantom power and sound pads in one box.

products.name: Elgato Wave XLR MK.2 USB interface and DSP mixer
products.description:
The MK.2 is the single voice sibling of the Wave XLR Pro: 80 dB of gain, an onboard voice enhancer, compressor and EQ, ultra low latency monitoring and an LED level display. It is the cleanest way to drive one demanding dynamic microphone.

It has one input and no faders, so it suits a solo streamer who sets levels once. Beside the Wave XLR Pro it offers the same voice chain for less money but no second microphone and fewer routing options.

Keep it on a stable USB port and revisit the DSP presets when you change microphones. Set the compressor to a gentle ratio first, then adjust the voice enhancer by ear on a recording rather than in the headphones alone. If you later add a second voice, the Wave XLR Pro keeps the same chain, so your settings carry across.
products.bestFor: Solo streamers with a demanding dynamic microphone.

products.name: FIFINE Ampligame SC3 XLR gaming mixer with Indi-Fader
products.description:
The SC3 is the minimal XLR box: one input, a slider, front mute and monitor buttons and plug and play USB. It gives a streamer a proper microphone path for very little money.

It does not mix game audio or add effects, so everything else stays in software. Next to the G1 Neo it skips phantom listing, Bluetooth and pads.

Use a balanced cable and a dynamic microphone, and mark the slider position. A dynamic microphone close to the mouth gives the best results in a gaming room full of fans and keyboard noise, and a pop filter costs little. When you outgrow the box, it remains useful as a travel interface for a laptop stream away from home.
products.bestFor: Solo streamers who want a simple XLR box with a mute button.
pros: One XLR input with a slider

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Elgato Wave XLR Pro and RØDECaster Duo offer two microphone inputs, while the Wave XLR MK.2, G3, G1 Neo and SC3 offer one. A co host needs the second input, and a solo streamer does not. Count real XLR jacks rather than channel labels.

Broadcast dynamic microphones need 60 to 70 dB of clean gain. The Elgato interfaces offer 80 dB per input and the Duo lists high gain preamps. A weak preamp forces you to boost in software, which raises noise.

Condenser microphones need 48V. The G1 Neo lists it, and the Duo's combo jacks serve both microphones and instruments. Confirm phantom support before pairing a condenser with any box. A condenser microphone is more sensitive and records keyboard clatter and room echo that a dynamic ignores, so it suits a quiet, treated space rather than a typical gaming desk.

Faders let you adjust levels without opening software. The RØDECaster Duo has four and the G3 has four mapped faders, while the Elgato boxes rely on software. Choose faders if you rebalance often. Each fader can be assigned to the source you reach for most, so a hand on the desk replaces a trip into software while a match is in progress.
The Wave XLR Pro offers dual USB-C and five hardware mixes, and the G3 supports a dual PC setup. If you stream from two machines or add a console, routing depth matters.
DSP in the box keeps compression and EQ off the computer. The Elgato units run a voice chain onboard. Hardware processing keeps your voice consistent even when the PC is busy.

howWeEvaluated.title: Microphone path
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared XLR input count, gain and phantom power. The Elgato interfaces lead on gain and the Duo on build. The microphone path is the foundation of a stream, so we weighed it above extras such as pads, lighting or Bluetooth, which suit entertainment channels but do not make a voice sound better.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control surface
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed faders, pads and software control, noting the Duo's four faders against the Elgato software approach. A streamer's hands are busy, so we valued controls that can be used by feel, and we noted that a software only mix costs nothing extra but takes attention from the audience.

howWeEvaluated.title: Routing
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at dual USB-C, submixes and hardware mixes. Independent mixes for the stream and for your headphones keep private alerts out of the broadcast, and a second USB link lets a console or another PC join without a capture card, so routing depth counted heavily for multi source desks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Processing
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked onboard DSP and protection against clipping. Processing in the box keeps the voice consistent when a game spikes the CPU, and clip protection helps with sudden shouts, so units with a hardware voice chain scored higher than those that leave every effect to software plug ins.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared price tiers, with the SC3 lowest and the Duo and Wave XLR Pro highest. Value depends on how many of a unit's features you will use, so a premium box earns its place only for a streamer who needs two inputs, deep routing or a full fader surface, while a basic box is better value for everyone else.

cards.label: Hardware faders
cards.text: The RØDECaster Duo and MAONO G3 give physical level control for a busy stream.

cards.label: Software mixing
cards.text: The Elgato interfaces keep the mix in software and spend hardware on gain and DSP.

howToChoose.note: Choose faders if you rebalance often and software if you set levels once.

cards.text: Two real XLR inputs, matched gain and separate headphone control.

cards.text: You host two people or want premium processing. The Wave XLR Pro or Duo reward that.

cards.text: You stream solo. The SC3 or G1 Neo covers the basics.

maintenance.why: Updates fix bugs and sometimes add routing features. Read the notes first, export your profile and update between streams rather than before one.
Connectors wear and cables fray at the strain relief. Wiggle each cable while listening on headphones and replace any that crackle, since a failing cable ruins a stream at the worst moment.
Dust and crumbs affect faders and pads on a busy desk. Use compressed air and a soft brush, and cover the unit when the stream ends.
Profiles restore your routing and processing after a reinstall or a new computer. Keep a dated copy on a drive other than the one running the stream.
Gain drifts when knobs are bumped, and a small change is easy to miss. Speak a test sentence at your normal volume and watch the meter before going live.

faq.a: XLR microphones sound better and reject noise, because the balanced cable cancels interference and the broadcast capsules used on streams pick up less of the room than a USB desktop microphone. They also let you upgrade or replace the microphone without changing the rest of the chain. The cost is a mixer or interface between the microphone and the computer.

faq.q: Do I need two XLR inputs?
faq.a: Only if you stream with a co host or invite guests often. A solo streamer needs one, and buying a second input adds cost and desk space for no benefit. The Wave XLR Pro and RØDECaster Duo carry two, and the others in this group carry one, so choose by the show you really run rather than the show you might run someday.

faq.q: Which is best for a solo streamer?
faq.a: The Elgato Wave XLR MK.2 is best if the voice is the priority, with 80 dB of gain and a voice chain in the box. The MAONO G3 is best if you juggle game, chat and music and want faders for each. The FIFINE SC3 is the budget choice when you only need a clean microphone path with a mute button.

Only for condenser microphones, which need 48V sent through the XLR cable. Dynamic microphones do not need it and are usually the better choice in a noisy room. The G1 Neo lists a 48V supply, and the Duo and Elgato boxes also handle microphones broadly, but check the manual for your exact microphone before connecting it.

They suit busy streams, where a hand on a fader is faster than a trip into a software panel. A streamer who balances game, chat and music every few minutes will appreciate them. One who sets levels once and then talks can save money with a software mixed interface.

faq.q: Can I use a second computer?
faq.a: The Wave XLR Pro and G3 support it, through dual USB-C and a dual PC setup respectively. A second computer keeps game and encoding load apart, and a mixer that connects to both avoids capture cards and virtual cables. Plan the routing before you buy, since each unit handles the second machine differently.
